html:
The Massacre of the Latins was a slaughter of the Western, mostly Italian, people of Constantinople in April 1182. Most victims were Genoese and Pisans, who then dominated the city's sea trade and banking; the Venetians had been driven out in the arrests of 1171.

After Manuel I died, the regent Maria of Antioch, herself a Latin, was seen as favouring the Italians. Resentment of their wealth, their privileges and their Catholic faith ran high. When Andronikos Komnenos marched on the capital, crowds attacked the Latin quarters. Thousands were killed, including women, children and the sick in hospital, and a papal envoy was among the dead. Many survivors were sold as slaves to the Turks. Some escaped by ship and plundered Greek coasts on the way home.

The massacre deepened the hatred between Latins and Greeks, and Westerners remembered it in 1204, when the crusaders sacked the city. It shows how the privileges that began with the Golden Bull had made Italians both rich and hated.
